1. What Poly-X is and what it is for

Poly-X is a software suite built to support the analysis of microplastics in samples stained with Nile Red under UV light (254 nm). Fluorescent staining makes it possible to tell polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polypropylene (PP) and low-density polyethylene (LDPE) apart by their characteristic colours under the microscope.

The suite has four main modules:

ModuleWhat it does
🔬 Detector Applies a trained YOLO model to your images and produces detections, metrics and a paper-quality report with error analysis and particle size in μm.
🎯 Trainer Trains your own YOLO v8 or v11 models from your labelled images. Live curves, automatic recommendations.
🏷 Labeler Annotates images in YOLO format (.txt). Supports pre-annotation with an existing model, which saves roughly 80% of the time.
📐 Viewer Viewer with precise per-particle measurement in μm.
Who is this program for? For researchers, students and laboratory technicians who need to quantify microplastics in environmental samples. No programming knowledge is required: everything is done through windows and clicks.

2. Installation and first run

2.1 Requirements

ComponentMinimumRecommended
Operating systemWindows 10Windows 11
Python3.11.x (NOT 3.12+)3.11.9
RAM8 GB16 GB
GPU—NVIDIA RTX (the installer picks the CUDA build)
Disk space5 GB10 GB
Important about Python: it must be 3.11.x (not 3.12 or 3.13). GPU acceleration (CUDA) requires this version. While installing Python, tick Add Python to PATH and tcl/tk and IDLE.

2.2 First installation (step by step)

  1. Install Python 3.11.9 from python.org. You must tick "Add Python to PATH" and "tcl/tk and IDLE".
  2. (Optional, if you have an NVIDIA GPU) install up-to-date NVIDIA drivers. CUDA itself is installed later, automatically.
  3. Double-click SETUP.bat. It creates the .venv virtual environment, detects the GPU and downloads PyTorch with the CUDA build that matches that card (~3-4 GB), or the CPU build. It takes 5-15 minutes the first time.
  4. GPU/PyTorch check. At the end it verifies that PyTorch ships kernels for your specific card. If it does not, it says so and explains how to reinstall the right wheel.
  5. Previous installations. If the machine already had Poly-X, its data is listed and you are offered to migrate it (see 2.4).
  6. When it finishes you will see "Instalación completada". You can close that window.
  7. To start using the program, double-click iniciar_polyx.bat.
RTX 50xx cards (Blackwell). These GPUs use the sm_120 architecture, which does not exist in PyTorch wheels built against CUDA 11.8. Installing the wrong wheel is particularly treacherous: torch.cuda.is_available() returns True, everything looks fine, and the failure only shows up during training as "no kernel image is available for execution on the device". The installer reads the card's compute capability and picks CUDA 12.8 from sm_120 upwards, so this is handled.

2.3 Everyday use

After installation, just double-click iniciar_polyx.bat and the main menu (launcher) opens. From there you reach any module with one click.

2.4 If the machine already had Poly-X

At the end of SETUP.bat, other installations on the machine are searched for. If one is found, its contents are shown —models, training runs, detections, datasets, with their size— and confirmation is requested by typing SI before anything is touched.

The order is copy → verify → remove, never the other way round:

  • Data the new installation does not already have is copied over. No existing file is overwritten.
  • If any copy fails, the old folder is kept untouched and you are told.
  • Only if everything went well is the old folder sent to the Recycle Bin. It is not deleted: if something is missing, restore it.
Folders containing .git are always skipped: a development repository is not an old installation, and removing it would take uncommitted work with it.

2.5 Updates

When the launcher opens, it checks in the background whether a newer version exists on GitHub. If so, an amber button appears in the top right with the version identifier; pressing it downloads and installs the update while preserving .venv, models, results and data.

The check does not delay start-up and stays quiet on any failure: with no internet, or with GitHub down, the notice simply does not appear. You can also force it with actualizar.bat.

3. Recommended workflow

There are two typical scenarios: use an already trained model (fast) or train your own model (more work, but tuned to your specific samples).

3.1 Scenario A: analyse new images with an existing model

  1. Open iniciar_polyx.bat.
  2. Click the 🔬 Detector card.
  3. In the Models tab, load bestdetectormedium.pt (included).
  4. In Images, select your folder of photos.
  5. In Parameters, set the μm/pixel calibration for your microscope.
  6. Click Run. You will see live progress.
  7. In Report, generate the paper-quality report.

3.2 Scenario B: train your own model from scratch

  1. Gather 200-500 representative images in a folder.
  2. Open the 🏷 Labeler and load the folder.
  3. Pre-annotate with bestdetectormedium.pt (saves ~80% of the time) and then review and correct each image.
  4. In the 🎯 Trainer, load your data.yaml, pick the "Balanced" preset and train.
  5. Once mAP@50 goes above 0.80, export the model and use it in the Detector.

Module 2

Detector — Microplastics analysis

Applies a trained YOLO model to your images and generates a paper-quality report. 8 tabs guide the flow.

5.1 Models tab

Here you load up to 3 .pt models. If you load more than one, the final report includes an automatic comparison.

Figure 2.1. Models tab. Three slots for loading .pt files with an editable alias.

How to use it:

  1. Click ... next to the ".pt" field to browse for the file.
  2. Change the alias to something descriptive ("YOLOv8m", "best fine-tuned", and so on).
  3. The "Use bestdetectormedium.pt" button under Quick load sets it up automatically as Model 1.

5.2 Images tab

Figure 2.2. Image loading. The "GT" column shows ✓ when a ground truth label is available.

How to use it:

  • 📷 Select images... to pick individual files.
  • 📁 Select folder... to load every image in a folder (recursively).
  • GT folder (optional): if you have ground truth labels in YOLO format (.txt) in a different folder, point to it. If left empty, the program looks for them next to each image and in a sibling labels/ folder.
Why load ground truth? Without GT you only see the model's detections. With GT the program computes TP/FP/FN, the confusion matrix, P/R/F1 and shows exactly which boxes failed. That is what makes the report publishable.

5.3 Parameters tab

Figure 2.3. Inference settings, IoU, calibration and filters.
ParameterWhat it doesTypical value
Minimum confidence Threshold for accepting a detection. 0.25 (general use), 0.50 (high precision)
NMS IoU Suppresses overlapping boxes. 0.45
TP matching IoU For error analysis (COCO standard). 0.50
μm per pixel Optical calibration of the microscope. Essential for reporting sizes. Depends on the objective. E.g. 0.244 μm/px at 40×.
Min/max size (μm) Discards detections outside the range. 0 = no filter

5.4 Run tab

Figure 2.4. Live processing: progress bar, step label and per-model preview.

Click ▶ Start detection. You will see:

  • Tiling notice: above the button it states whether the photos will be split into tiles, into how many, and how much longer it will take. A batch of full plates can take 12 times longer than a batch of crops, and it is better to know beforehand than two hours in.
  • Progress bar: batch progress.
  • Live preview (3 slots): the last image processed by each model, with its boxes drawn.
  • Stop button: cancels at any point without corrupting partial results.

Tiling does not change what you get. When a photo exceeds the threshold (2000 px by default), it is split into overlapping tiles only so that the model can detect: at full resolution the particles shrink below the network's stride and vanish. Boxes are returned in original photo coordinates and overlaps are merged with NMS, so results, annotated images and the report are always delivered on the complete photo, never on the tiles.

5.5 Results tab

Figure 2.5. Global metrics (TP/FP/FN/F1/precision/recall) and detailed per-image table.

Large KPI cards with the headline numbers, detailed metrics (precision, recall) and a table with every processed image (double-click to open the annotated image).

5.6 Errors tab

Figure 2.6. List of every box with an error. Filter by type (FP/FN/MISCLS).

Only active when ground truth is available. It lists every problematic box:

  • FP False positives: the model detected something where there was nothing.
  • FN False negatives: there is an object in GT but the model missed it.
  • MISCLS Located correctly (IoU ≥ 0.5) but assigned the wrong class.

5.7 Compare tab

Figure 2.7. Comparison table of the loaded models plus per-image agreement.

If you loaded more than one model, here you get a summary table with all metrics side by side and how many detections each one made per image.

5.8 Report tab (THE IMPORTANT ONE)

Figure 2.8. Paper-quality HTML report generator.

The Detector's main output. Click 📄 Generate HTML report and reporte_paper.html is created inside the run folder. It contains:

  1. Abstract with detections, mean confidence and mean size.
  2. Methods: model, parameters, calibration, device, date.
  3. General results: class distribution, confidence histogram, size distribution (μm), per-class table with P/R/F1.
  4. Per-model summary table.
  5. Error analysis: confusion matrix, P/R/F1 per class, gallery of the images with most errors.
  6. Model comparison: a photo-by-photo table with each model's detections and, when ground truth exists, their TP/FP/FN and the overall F1.
  7. Full gallery of annotated images.
  8. References.

Scope: which photos go into the report

In the Report scope card you choose between three options:

  • Whole job: every analysed photo.
  • Only the photos you tick: they are listed below with checkboxes, plus buttons to tick or untick all.
  • Both: generates the two reports at once. The selection one carries the _seleccion suffix so it does not overwrite the complete one.

Figures, charts and the confusion matrix are recomputed over the chosen photos. If only the gallery were filtered, the totals would describe one batch and the images another, and the report would contradict itself.

If you ask for a report of specific photos and tick none, you get a warning instead of an empty report, which would read as if nothing had been detected.

Export to PDF

The 📑 Export to PDF button renders with the browser engine (QtWebEngine) and respects the chosen scope: with Both you get two PDFs. If QtWebEngine is unavailable, generate the HTML and use Ctrl+P → "Save as PDF".

Both the HTML and the PDF are self-contained: images are embedded, so they do not break when you send them to someone else.

Model comparison

It pays to look at the photo-by-photo table and not just the total. In uneven batches —such as the Loa river cores, where a single depth interval holds most of the particles— that interval decides the total on its own and can hide that the other model wins everywhere else.

No winner is declared without ground truth. A model with more detections may be getting them right or may be inventing them, and without annotations there is no way to tell.

Module 3

Trainer — YOLO v8 / v11 models

To build your own model from a labelled dataset. 9 tabs guide you from choosing the architecture to the final report.

6.1 Model

Figure 3.1. YOLO family and size selection, or custom weights.

Pick a preset ("Balanced" is recommended), family (v8 or v11) and size. Each size has a description and a colour badge.

Comparing architectures on equal terms

The "Train both architectures (v8 and v11) with the same configuration" checkbox trains both, one after the other, reusing exactly the same imgsz, batch, epochs, seed and augmentation. When ticked, the family selector is disabled: it no longer applies, because both are trained.

  • The configuration is resolved once and imposed on both runs. That is what lets you attribute a difference in metrics to the architecture rather than to the hyperparameters.
  • They run in sequence, not in parallel: they share the GPU, and running them together would slow each other down and distort the timings. It takes twice as long.
  • Each run is saved with its family suffix (…_v8, …_v11), so the second does not overwrite the first.
  • At the end, the log summarises the comparison: mAP@50 for each, the epoch of the best checkpoint, and which one won.

With a single training run per architecture, a small difference does not separate the network design from initialisation randomness. Claiming one is better would require repetitions with different seeds.

If you load custom weights, the comparison is ignored: that .pt already fixes one architecture. The program says so in the log.

The weight that works on your photos: best_real.pt

The "Pick the best weight by field photos, not laboratory ones" checkbox is enabled by default, and solves a problem that would otherwise go unnoticed.

Ultralytics saves best.pt according to the mAP of the full validation split. In a mixed dataset that number is dominated by the laboratory spiked plates: few images, but very dense. In the Loa dataset, validation holds 1191 laboratory boxes against 47 of real sediment — 96% of the wrong domain. Left alone, you would walk away with the checkpoint that performs best on clean plates, which is precisely the domain that does not transfer to field photos.

With the checkbox enabled, after each training run every saved checkpoint (best, last and the periodic ones) is evaluated against only the real sediment images, and the winner is copied as best_real.pt.

  • Selection is by F1, with mAP50 as tie-breaker: counting depends on getting the number of particles right, not on refining the box.
  • best.pt is left untouched: both weights remain, and the report can state which one was used.
  • The log shows the table of all checkpoints and says whether the re-selection changed the weight with respect to best.pt.
  • If the re-selection fails for any reason, you are told and it falls back to best.pt: a failure here must not throw away hours of training.

To detect on field photos, load the best_real.pt weights, not the best.pt ones. With architecture comparison enabled you get one per family, and the final comparison in the log uses the F1 on real sediment — the number that describes what those weights will actually do in the field.

Domains are told apart by the filename prefix (real__ and lab__) written by armar_dataset.py. If your dataset does not carry both, the step is skipped silently.

6.2 Dataset

Figure 3.2. Loading data.yaml, preview with boxes and the auto-split tool.

Load your data.yaml. The program validates the structure, counts images/labels per split and offers a preview with boxes drawn. If you only have an undivided folder, use auto-split to create train/val automatically.

6.3 Parameters

Figure 3.3. Parameters with tooltips (?) and automatic recommendations.

Every field has a ? icon with an explanation. The bottom panel shows recommendations based on your hardware and dataset.

6.4 Augmentation

Figure 3.4. Data augmentation: HSV, mixup, copy-paste.

Preconfigured levels (Light/Medium/Strong) or manual sliders. Useful for small datasets (< 500 images).

6.5 Train

Figure 3.5. Live mAP/loss/precision/recall curves during training.

The ▶ Start training button launches the process. You will see:

  • Live metrics (8 cards: epoch, mAP@50, mAP@50-95, P, R, loss, best, epochs without improvement).
  • Live matplotlib curves (2×2: box loss, mAP, precision, recall).
  • Early-stopping indicator (epochs without improvement vs patience).
  • Full Ultralytics log.

6.6 Evaluate

Figure 3.6. Validating any .pt against a YOLO dataset without retraining.

6.7 Compare

Figure 3.7. Table of all previous runs with their final metrics and an A+ to F grade.

6.8 Export

Figure 3.8. Converts the model to ONNX, TensorRT, TFLite, CoreML, etc.

Module 4

Labeler — YOLO annotation

To label your own images in YOLO format. Supports automatic pre-annotation.

Figure 4.1. Labeler main view. Image list on the left, central canvas with the image and boxes, class panel on the right.

7.1 Basic steps

  1. Click 📂 Open folder... and choose the folder with your images.
  2. Pick a class preset ("Nile Red microplastics" = PET/PP/LDPE) or add classes manually.
  3. (STRONGLY RECOMMENDED) Click 🤖 Pre-annotate with model → "Pre-annotate ALL". The model labels automatically and you only have to correct.
  4. For each image: drag the mouse to draw boxes. Right-clicking a box assigns the active class to it.
  5. Use ← → to navigate (autosaves on change).

7.2 Keyboard shortcuts

ShortcutAction
← → Previous/next image (autosaves)
1 ... 9 Change active class
Del Delete selected box
Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y Undo / Redo
Ctrl+S Save (also saves when changing image)
Mouse wheelZoom
Middle mouse buttonPan (move the image)
Right clickAssigns the active class to the box
YOLO .txt files are saved automatically next to each image (or in a sibling labels/ folder if the image lives under images/). A classes.txt is also created at the root of your folder — ready to use in the Trainer.

Module 5

Viewer with measurement

Inspect one image at a time with interactive μm/pixel calibration and precise per-particle measurement.

Figure 5.1. Viewer main view. Canvas with the image on the left and control panel on the right.

8.1 What it does and when to use it

The viewer is the detailed inspection tool: one image at a time, focused on optical calibration and precise measurement. It complements the Detector, which is built for batch processing.

8.2 Interactive μm/pixel calibration

This is the key feature the Detector does not have. In the right-hand panel pick one of these modes:

  • 📏 Line (2 clicks) — Click two points on a known reference (for example a ruler mark in the image) and type its real size (in μm or mm).
  • ⭕ Circle (3 clicks) — Click three points on the edge of a known circular object (calibration sphere, eyepiece). The viewer computes the circle through those 3 points and asks for the real diameter.

The resulting μm/pixel is stored and applied automatically to every detection measurement. It appears in the bottom bar: "📐 0.4880 μm/px (line)".

8.3 Recommended flow

  1. Load your .pt model in the right-hand panel and press "Load model into memory".
  2. Open an image (📷) or a folder (📁). With a folder, navigate with ← →.
  3. Calibrate: click "📏 Line" or "⭕ Circle", mark the reference on the image and enter its real size.
  4. Press ▶ Detect. Boxes appear over the image with their class number and size in μm.
  5. Review the table on the right (filter by class with the combo).
  6. 💾 Save current info exports a folder with the annotated image at full resolution, a CSV of every detection with all its measurements, and a JSON summary.

8.4 Keyboard shortcuts

ShortcutAction
← →Previous/next image
Ctrl+DDetect on the current image
Mouse wheelZoom
Middle mouse buttonPan (move the image)
EscCancel calibration mode
Right click while calibratingCancel the calibration in progress
Difference from the Detector: the Detector processes many images and produces the paper-style report, but needs you to know the μm/px beforehand. The Viewer computes that μm/px by clicking on the image itself, which is the natural approach when your microscope burns a visible scale into every photo.

9. Shortcuts and practical advice

9.1 To speed up the workflow

  • Pre-annotate before labelling by hand. The labeler can use your current model to label every image automatically; you only fix mistakes. Saves around 80% of the time.
  • Use a GPU if you have one. Training is 20-30× faster on GPU than on CPU. Check that nvidia-smi works and that SETUP.bat detected the GPU.
  • Start from presets. "Balanced" works well for most cases. Do not touch parameters without understanding what they do.

9.2 For better metrics

  • More data beats a bigger model. 500 well-labelled images with the Balanced preset beat 100 images with an XL model.
  • Balance the classes. With 80% PET and 5% LDPE the model will skew towards PET. Aim for at least 30%-30%-30%.
  • Optical calibration. Measure your μm/pixel against a known reference (calibration slide) before applying it in the detector. It is essential for reporting correct sizes.

9.3 For publishable reports

  • Label a test set with ground truth. Without GT you have no error metrics and the report is not publishable.
  • Compare at least 2 models. Papers never report a model in isolation — always against a baseline.
  • Convert the HTML report to PDF. To submit to journals: open in Chrome → Ctrl+P → "Save as PDF" → minimum margins.

10. Troubleshooting

10.1 Common errors

No module named 'tkinter'

Your Python 3.11 was installed without the tcl/tk component. Fix: download python-3.11.9-amd64.exe, run it and choose "Modify". Tick "tcl/tk and IDLE" and apply.

CUDA not available (a warning, not an error)

Training runs on CPU, but it is very slow. Check: up-to-date NVIDIA drivers, Python 3.11.x (not 3.12+), and that SETUP.bat ran correctly.

no kernel image is available for execution on the device

PyTorch does not ship kernels for your GPU architecture. It is the typical symptom of an RTX 50xx card with a CUDA 11.8 build. Reinstall with the right wheel:

.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --force-reinstall torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128

The detector finds nothing (zero boxes)

  • Confidence too high — lower it to 0.10 to test.
  • The model was not trained for your samples — pre-annotate with bestdetectormedium.pt and review.
  • Very low resolution or very noisy images.
  • Large photos without tiling: check the tiling notice in the Run tab.

Training runs out of memory (OOM)

  • Lower batch to 4 or 2.
  • Lower imgsz from 1280 to 640.
  • Use a smaller model (m → s, or s → n).
  • Enable AMP in the parameters.

The labeler cannot find the model for pre-annotation

By default it looks for bestdetectormedium.pt in the project folder. If it is not there, set the path manually in the "PRE-ANNOTATION MODEL" field of the right-hand panel.

11. References

The detection method by Nile Red fluorescence under UV light (254 nm) and the visual identification of polymers are based on the following works published by the author:

  2. Ferrada C, Pérez M, Parra S, Salas E, Sepúlveda F, Bravo MA, Quiroz W (2024).
